topics.title: About our Continuous Tension Method
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 5 - Continuous Tension Method/Academy - Continuous Tension Method 1 - About our Continuous Tension Method.txt

blocks.text: In setting out to develop our training protocol, safety was the primary concern. Therefore a slower, smoother movement pace that minimizes momentum and sudden forces was adopted. A slower, continuous speed of movement will also ensure a more orderly recruitment and sustained overlapping of muscle fibers (actin and myosin cross-bridges). This creates the possibility for more mechanical tension due to the force-velocity relationship, which dictates that a muscle fiber exerts higher levels of force at slower contraction speeds.

Our execution of directional changes is of even greater importance under our methodology. An exaggerated control with a high level of focus is required to ensure continuous movement with no pause (from eccentric to concentric) or acceleration. While this does make for a more technically challenging execution that requires a higher level of motor control, it more importantly creates a safer approach to strength training. It is often the change of direction in an exercise (and sports for that matter) where dangerous sudden forces are introduced. Along with the gradual load up, if a subject attempts to precisely control the changes of direction, they will accomplish a majority of what it takes to properly perform our Continuous Tension Protocol.

This careful control combined with a high degree of effort is a challenging but rewarding endeavor for both the client and the instructor. The Exercise Practitioner and client will grow together in their expertise and abilities making this a lifelong learning process full of enriching experiences along the way. The trainee becomes more trusting of and reliant on the trainer to ensure progress and the trainer becomes more insightful and appreciative of the trainee's accomplishments.

topics.title: What Makes the Continuous Tension Method Effective
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 5 - Continuous Tension Method/Academy - Continuous Tension Method 2 - What Makes the Continuous Tension Method Effective_.txt

blocks.text: What Makes the Continuous Tension Method Effective?

Safe and efficient muscular loading—via high mechanical tension—is the defining feature of the MSF protocol. Continuous Tension repetitions minimize momentum, which otherwise reduces tension on the target musculature. As momentum is controlled, tension progressively increases until the nervous system can no longer recruit additional motor units. At this point, contraction velocity (internal) and external movement speed involuntarily slow. This involuntary slowing indicates full motor unit recruitment and peak effort, where target fibers experience meaningful mechanical tension. These repetitions are referred to as stimulating (productive/effective) reps.

It is important to note here that "full motor unit recruitment" is a relative term and is highly specific to the individual. It is unlikely that a person is truly able to recruit 100% of their motor units involved in a given movement. And, in general, more experienced trainees will be able to recruit more of their motor units than newer trainees.

In an effort to maintain a continuous pace, the trainee should begin to push/pull harder (voluntarily increase effort), thus attempting additional effective reps leading to an increase in stimulus-inducing mechanical tension. During this critical time in a set, it needs to be reinforced that the trainee and instructor are still focused on quality and attempting to maintain a pace between 6 and 10 seconds.

A conservative estimate of an approximate 6-second concentric/eccentric is the minimum cadence that will truly control momentum for most subjects. Importantly, this is really just a guideline that has been established with the primary goal of client safety in mind. There is no “magic” in the number itself. And while some research may suggest that intentionally slow movements are not necessarily more stimulative, they are undoubtedly safer. This is reason enough to adopt a controlled movement approach. Furthermore, if the client is properly informed and directed, they will eventually get to the more beneficial, involuntary slow reps soon after they commence a set of exercise using our Continuous Tension method.

A 10-second pace is the maximum. Going slower than 10 seconds can cause the movement to become segmented, and portions of a movement may become a respite giving some of the active fibers a chance to recover. In addition, an unusually slow pace will lead to higher levels of discomfort, causing the trainee to prematurely reach task failure. Essentially, the discomfort is the reason for terminating the set, thus stopping short of a fully stimulated muscle. (Note: task failure is the preferred physiological term for what used to be called “muscular failure”. This distinction was necessary because subjects do not reach failure because their muscles fail. Instead, they decide to stop performing the task because of information sent to the brain from the periphery based on the intensity of the activity. This is a protective mechanism to prevent the subject from running out of ATP, which would be deadly).

While there is not exactly one ideal pace for exercise, somewhere between 6 and 10 seconds should result in a movement that minimizes momentum and avoids a respite and unproductive discomfort. Again it is important to note that different trainees will gravitate to different ends of the ranges. Ultimately the clients should be empowered to control their movement and fully understand what productive training requires. These are attributes that can be refined and progressed for a lifetime and it will be the responsibility of a highly skilled Exercise Practitioner to develop insight to help guide this process.

More important than the actual speed of the movement, is establishing and keeping control of the resistance. Each exercise has different ranges of motion. Some exercises, like the Pullover, have a long range of motion compared to the shorter stroke of a Calf Raise. Naturally, the shorter range of motion of the calf exercise requires less time for a repetition. Also of note are the differences in limb length of clients, which will lead to different distances moved for a given exercise. Someone with longer legs would most likely be expected to have a longer excursion time on a leg press than someone with shorter legs. These are also reasons for having an acceptable range of 6 to 10 seconds rather than one specific cadence.

The challenge for the trainee is to "feel" what proper control is under extreme stress. And to become more adept over time at having an awareness of all of the details that the Continuous Tension method requires. The challenge for the instructor is to be able to observe and interpret movement and effort and provide meaningful, timely instruction to direct the client. This, along with safety, are the main reasons someone should be supervised during productive exercise.

Learning our Continuous Tension method requires more engagement and effort than just merely going in and lifting weights. It requires steadfast concentration and disciplined practice and, more importantly, skilled instruction. This is yet another way a MSF Exercise Practitioner distinguishes themselves in the industry.

A properly performed MaxStrength Fitness exercise session is anything but fun. It is extremely challenging and can involve a high degree of discomfort. But productive exercise has to be this way. The human body is a stubborn and efficient organism that would rather not exert at these high levels or build new strength and muscle. It is too metabolically expensive. But if one can learn to appreciate the details in the process and rise to the challenge, the physical and mental benefits will be well worth the effort.

topics.title: Performing the Continuous Tension Method
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 5 - Continuous Tension Method/Academy - Continuous Tension Method 3 - Performing the Continuous Tension Method.txt

blocks.text: A Continuous Tension repetition involves lifting the resistance in 6 to 10 seconds (the positive or concentric phase of movement) and lowering the resistance in 6 to 10 seconds (the negative or eccentric phase of movement). Every effort should be made to maintain a constant pace in both directions of a movement with a potentially slower cadence used for beginners or those with an injury or other physical compromise.

An emphasis is placed on the most contracted position on movements that are rotary (single-joint exercises). On most exercises that are compound (more than one joint movement), a continuous smooth motion should occur. The change in direction from the negative phase to the positive (called the "lower turnaround") should be smooth and controlled. In some cases, it may be advisable to actually slow down a faster-paced eccentric as one approaches the lower turnaround in order to maintain the exaggerated control we require that is void of momentum or a pause. This will also serve to keep the muscles under a constant level of tension and create a safer set of exercise.

The Exercise Practitioner must develop a keen eye for movement quality in order to provide meaningful and timely instruction to ensure exercise accuracy and safety, particularly involving the pace and changes of direction. This instruction becomes even more valuable and critical further into a set where a client may experience discomfort or duress. While the encouragement of effort is definitely part of an instructor's role, this should never overshadow the encouragement of safety and control. The true challenge for an advanced client is to execute with the highest level of intensity (effort) while maintaining strict control of the movement. To teach clients to operate in this manner and to be able to progress both of these variables becomes the true challenge for the instructor as well.

The number of repetitions or set duration is a controlling factor in determining how much resistance would be optimal for any given trainee. Any less than 5 repetitions and the resistance is most likely too heavy. Now for an advanced client, 4 or 5 reps may be an appropriately loaded set but most would benefit from a slightly lighter load that allows for potentially better control. Sets performed with upwards of 12 or more reps tend to create higher levels of discomfort leading to higher levels of perceived effort. This ultimately leads to a greater degree of fatigue, which decreases motor unit recruitment thus minimizing the potential stimulus. Not only that, but maintaining focus and quality are made more difficult with longer duration sets. Keep in mind however, that this lighter weight and higher repetition count may be useful for beginners or injured clients or even intensity-adverse trainees. But in order to stimulate the muscle to change, it needs to be challenged with a high degree of mechanical tension and a limited amount of fatigue. This is best accomplished and supported in the literature as a set of somewhere between 5 and 10 repetitions taken to or near muscular failure.

Some trainees achieve better results and are more compliant at the upper end of the repetition range, while others need and thrive on fewer repetitions. Again, this is part of the ever-evolving skill set of the Exercise Practitioner to discern what approach to take or to at least be able to facilitate what clients relate better to what strategy.

topics.title: Other Factors to Consider
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 5 - Continuous Tension Method/Academy - Continuous Tension Method 4 - Other Factors to Consider.txt

blocks.text: In addition to the pace of the movement and the handling of the changes of direction, several other factors must be implemented in order to properly perform our protocol. The most important of the other factors is the prevention of the Valsalva maneuver. The Valsalva is an instinctive mechanism whereby the subject will hold their breath while simultaneously exerting physically. It's a protective measure taken by the body to provide rigidity through the torso that allows for a brief increase in force production. This oftentimes goes unnoticed and again is instinctive.

Take for instance, a situation where someone is going to pick up a heavy bag of mulch in the backyard or is about to lift a small child. At that moment, they will hold their breath and possibly let out a small grunt as they complete their task. If this breath-holding is maintained for a duration, there are a host of potential negative consequences associated with this. Among them are increased blood pressure and altered cardiac output.

For our purposes, we're looking to sustain a muscular effort for a period of time that exceeds a brief moment. In order to do this, one needs to breathe the entire time, especially as the duration, and thus effort, increases. By doing so, the trainee will maintain safe levels of their internal environment and they will be able to use less weight making the exercise safer. By avoiding this bracing mechanism that breath holding provides, a lighter weight will "feel" heavier and there will be a more direct loading of the targeted muscles.

Our clients are instructed to breathe freely for the duration of the exercise, and those respirations should actually increase with exertion. It is very similar to what happens when you walk up several flights of stairs; as you climb higher, the muscles are working harder, so the heart and lungs increase their function as well as our breathing increases to support the effort. This may be the most challenging aspect of the Continuous Tension method for a trainee to master because they are having to overcome a programmed instinct. In any event, the instructor needs to reiterate the importance of breathing and must enforce its compliance.

Another component of our protocol to consider is that of the anatomical positioning or posture for each exercise. Each exercise has an ideal posture that will ensure safety as well as proper and direct loading of the targeted musculature. For single-joint movements, the axis of rotation of the machine should be aligned with the center of the joint that is being used. Compound exercises have a more theoretical alignment that do not necessarily seek to match a part of the machine with a part of the body. These need to be considered on a machine-to-machine and client-by-client basis and should become part of the Exercise Practitioner's skill set.

These obvious positioning elements aside, the actual posture assumed on each exercise is critical. For the most part, our exercises will utilize one of two general postures, a posterior pelvic tilt or an anterior pelvic tilt. A posterior pelvic tilt requires a contracted abdomen (not necessarily "drawn in") whereby the bottom of the front of the ribcage is brought closer toward the top of the front of the pelvis and vice versa. This is accomplished through a contraction of the rectus abdominis. An anterior pelvic tilt is simply lifting the front of the ribcage away from the pelvis. This is accomplished by lifting the chest and creating a slight arch in the lower back.

When a trainee is positioned at the beginning of an exercise, this is called the "get-set."  The trainee is expected to "lock" this posture in place. In most cases, part of the benefit of the exercise is the effort it takes to maintain the get-set posture. This is also something that the instructor to watch for and preemptively cue as a reminder for the client.

A primary component of the posture on any given movement involves the placement of the head. Most of the time, the trainee will maintain what's referred to as a neutral head and neck position; this balances the tension around the neck muscles to share more equally in the support of the head. This is especially critical during moments of exertion where the risk of straining is greatly increased. Clients should maintain a still, neutral head and neck for the duration of the exercise.

There are exceptions to the posture restraints on movements involving flexion, extension, or rotation of the trunk or the cervical extension exercise. But for a majority of exercises, the trainee should expect and be challenged and reminded to keep their ribcage and head still!

topics.title: Athletic Performance
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 5 - Continuous Tension Method/Academy - Continuous Tension Method 5 - Athletic Performance.txt

blocks.text: Many will wonder if the Continuous Tension method will hinder athletic performance. The answer is absolutely not! In fact, it will only enhance sports performance. Any increases in strength and/or improvement in body composition as a result of strength training will improve functional ability and, therefore, athletic performance. Simply stated, a stronger person is a more capable person.

Sports performance, like any physical endeavor, requires varying degrees of skill. Skill in a sport is the ability to perform precision movements at the right time, successfully, regularly, and with minimal effort. By strengthening the muscles, an athlete will have better control of fast movements, will be able to perform them more easily, and will increase their resistance to injury.

Research has shown that strength gains made with a fast speed of movement are not transferable to slower speeds. But strength gains made with a slow speed of movement are carried over to a faster speed of movement. It should also be noted here that when strength training intensely and at near maximal effort, oftentimes the speed of the movement itself is slow despite the trainee's intent to move faster. It is this INTENT to move faster that creates the training stimulus we seek in the form of effective reps.

The significance of that research is the discovery that fast movements are skill-dependent (Tai Chi Chuan practitioners have known that for two thousand years). Strength is not actually increased with fast speeds, which makes sense if you consider that a heavy or challenging load relative to the trainee's capabilities cannot be moved fast. This would be the same situation with a fatigued trainee, near muscular failure; the load would not be able to be accelerated. And if a load can be moved fast or accelerated, there is an introduction of momentum, which we have previously pointed out will decrease mechanical tension. So when we take these things into consideration, we realize that skill is increased and is limited by general strength. The strength gained at slower speeds can be used with any activity, and it can enhance skills requiring fast movements.

To say it another way, the skill level of a movement is limited by the strength of the muscles being used to perform that movement. Increase the strength and the potential for skill increase is made available. The strength increase does not guarantee an increase in skill, however. The skill must be continually rehearsed for an improvement to be made.

Research has also shown that strength will increase only if a muscle is stimulated according to that muscle’s function. Attempting to improve a skill by mimicking that skill in an exercise fashion will not increase the skill. It may, in fact, undermine and inhibit the skill. The mimicked motion is enhanced, but not the actual motion.
